AJK.name: Juneau
AJK.excerpt: Confidence is high on cold air moving in at the surface Monday, along with moisture timing Tuesday and Wednesday. Largest uncertainty is how warm will the incoming airmass be and how quickly we can scrub out any persistent cold air at the surface.

sections.name: Evening, Aviation, And Long Term Forecast Update
paragraphs: No major changes to ongoing forecast this evening. Winds remain light widespread across the panhandle and inner channels, strongest being Eldred Rock northerly around 10 to 15kts. With a weakening system pushing inland, ceilings remain low across much of the panhandle, with areas of patchy fog possible into the early morning hours for any areas that see the slightest bit of clearing. Otherwise, relatively benign, but wet conditions continue. A weak front pushes into the panhandle Friday morning followed up by a stronger, more seasonal front into the panhandle by Friday night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: /Sunday through Wednesday/... Sunday continues to look like one fine day across Southeast, with the potential for some fog development. Stay tuned. Mariners moving around the inner channels should be aware of outflow winds, especially overnight into Monday as high pressure builds across the Yukon and BC provinces. One impact from outflow will be cold air once again infiltrating the Panhandle, especially those closest to the Coast Range and major river inlets, priming us for snow. Expect a large system to move in off the Bering Monday steering plenty of moisture into our area Tuesday into Wednesday. Snow impacts will be directly tied to how prolific the outflow event is for the start of next week, the resulting cold air infiltration, and how quickly relatively warmer southerlies can scrub out the cold airmass at the surface. For now, the published forecast reflects minor snow for some communities separate from Haines and Skagway. It certainly feels like the first snow event for us humble few in Southeast; however, accumulating snow (outside of the Haines and Klondike highways) looks modest, likely only some flakes to perhaps an inch before turning to rain. Yakutat will also see some snow Tuesday. Stay tuned as we monitor for developments thru the weekend.

Confidence is high on cold air moving in at the surface Monday, along with moisture timing Tuesday and Wednesday. Largest uncertainty is how warm will the incoming airmass be and how quickly we can scrub out any persistent cold air at the surface. While it looks like a decent overrunning setup, the limiting factor is the duration of the Monday outflow, limiting snow potential.

sections.name: Prev Discussion
paragraphs: ...ISSUED AT 345 PM AKST Thu Nov 26 2026...
- Continued periods of light rain for Icy Strait Corridor and southward for Thanksgiving and Friday.
- Another system moves in for Friday night into Saturday, bringing slightly increased winds and more rain from Yakutat to around Sumner Strait.
- Drier and cooler weather for Sunday with fog chances for Saturday into Sunday.

Somewhat more benign forecast for Thanksgiving and going into this weekend. The weakening low moving up from the south is converting into an open wave trough, with a bulk of the upper air support far south of the panhandle. What is left is a broad hole of divergence, which is helping keep rain in the forecast for a majority of the panhandle. While plenty of moisture is available, available lift and weak winds in the lower levels does not look to bring any rainfall intensities higher than moderate, except for possibly the extreme southern panhandle during the evening hours.

Going into Friday morning, stronger cold air advection and just enough frontogensis looks to bring a weak, lower level trough to move over the panhandle from NW to SE, once again increases those rain chances. In its wake, a stronger through will sweep across the gulf waters, Friday night and into Saturday morning, weakening around the Yakutat area. Looking to see Yakutat get a bulk of the rainfall, less than a half inch, with the Icy Strait down to Sumner Strait having the highest likelihood to see measurable precip to roughly a quarter inch precipitation. Haines, Skagway, and the highways are not expected to receive much precipitation at this time, as stronger westerly to southwesterly winds are expected to shadow over the Chilkat Range. If any areas does see some snow accumulation, less than 2 inches, it would be on the Klondike Highway.

MARINE... Outer Waters: Overall offshore NE flow is expected to decrease and shift to the west late Thursday night and increase to about 15-20kts as a weak front moves up from the south into early Friday morning. Winds are expected to peak Friday afternoon before diminishing slightly, 10-15kts ahead of another front. Winds shift to the south late Friday as another front approaches the gulf. Winds are not anticipated to build much more than 15-20kts as this secondary front approaches. Behind the front on Saturday morning, winds then shift to the northwest as high pressure builds into the area.

Inner Channels: Conditions across the inner channels are generally settling with Lynn Canal and Stephens Passage remaining elevated around 15kts. Through the evening, these conditions are expected to become less than 10kts. By Friday morning, a shift in pattern brings south to southeast winds as a front approaches from the south. This front is likely to bring elevated winds up to 20kts mainly across southern inner channels, especially east/west oriented channels. Winds are expected to peak last Friday night before diminishing. Winds across the northern panhandle build Friday night as another front moves across the area, especially in north/south oriented channels. Overall, winds diminish again through the day Saturday as high pressure moves into the gulf.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The aforementioned trough will swing through the forecast area on Monday, with gusty winds and periods of showers continuing throughout the day. Snow levels will gradually lower as the trough passes, down to 5500-6500 ft by Monday afternoon.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Periods of valley rain and mountain snow today through early Saturday, with warm temperatures raising snow levels to 6500-8500 feet.
- Gusty winds in southern areas, and heavy rain possible with cold frontal passage this evening into Saturday morning.
- Unsettled pattern continues with above normal temperatures through next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Precipitation will expand across northeast Oregon and west- central/central Idaho later this morning as a significant moisture plume funnels into the area. Strong westerly winds aloft will favor orographic lift across the West-Central ID and Boise Mountains throughout the day, while some valley locations become susceptible to shadowing effects. Mild temperatures will keep snow levels high at around 6000-7000 ft MSL across the north, and 8000-9000 ft farther south. The plume of moisture will gradually sag south and east by this afternoon/evening as an upper level trough carries in a cold front. As a result, precipitation will spread into the rest of southeast Oregon and through southwest Idaho. Heaviest precip amounts will continue for higher terrain, with snow accumulations reaching 5-10 inches above 7500-8500 ft associated with 0.50-1.00 inches of liquid equivalent.

Late today into early Saturday, the strong mid-level winds and tightening surface pressure gradient will support 30-50 mph gusts over the higher terrain and portions of the Treasure and Magic Valleys with the cold front. Precipitation will become convective during this time, allowing for bursts of heavier rain/snow showers. Expect precip to end from north to south tonight into Saturday morning as a drier airmass follows behind the cold front. Winds will also gradually taper off for most areas, but continue across south-central Idaho through Saturday morning. The rest of Saturday is expected to remain dry as brief ridging develops. Cooler overnight temperatures and precedent moisture will allow patchy/areas of fog development in sheltered valleys Saturday night into Sunday morning.

The next trough will arrive in the Pacific Northwest Sunday, bringing warm frontal precipitation into the forecast area by the afternoon. Snow levels will rise to 6000-7500 ft during this time, climbing further by Sunday night, and winds will increase across southeast Oregon and the higher terrain of southwest Idaho. Temperatures will remain above normal through the rest of the weekend.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The aforementioned trough will swing through the forecast area on Monday, with gusty winds and periods of showers continuing throughout the day. Snow levels will gradually lower as the trough passes, down to 5500-6500 ft by Monday afternoon. Showers will taper off Monday night as the trough exits toward the northeast. Beginning early Tuesday, there is general guidance agreement on a plume of moisture steering into our area from the south by a deep upper low digging into the California coast. The exact magnitude and extent of precipitation remains slightly uncertain. For now, the area will see the return of moderate to high precipitation chances through most of Tuesday. Troughing from this upper low will bring a slight cooling trend on Tuesday, dropping snow levels into the 5000-6500 ft MSL range from north to south. As such, the central ID mountains will see better chances of light snow accumulations between 2 to 4 inches Tuesday morning through early afternoon. Precipitation will taper off to the east come Tuesday evening as the upper low steers further east across the Great Basin. Wednesday through early Thursday, a positively tilted ridge will build in behind the upper low, keeping our area dry. Temperatures are looking to hover near seasonal normals Wednesday through Thursday, with snow levels staying in the 4000-5000 ft MSL range. A relatively weak upper trough will dig into the Pacific northwest region Thursday through Friday, with considerable uncertainty on precipitation timing and extend. For now, Thursday through early Friday will see the return of low to moderate valley rain and mountain snow chances areawide. Temperatures will stay near or slightly below normal through Friday.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Snow chances will decrease Saturday evening as the shortwave and jet move out of our area. Dry conditions will prevail Sunday through Tuesday for much of the area, with warmer temperature for the start of next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Hazardous travel Friday night - Saturday evening for the northern mountains and I-70 mountain corridor due to snow and blowing snow. Local snowfall amounts greater than 12" possible.

- Banded rain/snow for the the plains and I-25 Corridor Saturday to Saturday evening. Brief heavy snow with generally light accumulations possible, including potential for Denver's first measurable snowfall of the season.
- Gusty winds expected along the northern Front Range and northern border area Friday, spreading to all the plains Saturday.
- Return of mostly dry weather Sunday - Tuesday, next disturbance may arrive by Wednesday or Thursday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The system for this weekend is still on track. We're starting to see winds increase in the higher terrain, with gusts around 30 to 50mph already. Northwest flow aloft will continue to strengthen through Friday afternoon, remaining strong through late Saturday. Wind gusts above tree line will be around 50 to 70mph late Friday morning through the early afternoon. The strongest winds will be confined to the highest elevations, but wind gusts will still reach around 30 to 50mph in the northern foothills. The strong northwest winds are expected to move off of the Cheyenne Ridge and into our northern counties in the early morning, producing gusts around 30 to 50mph in the northern plains.

While snow could start in the mountains on Friday, the peak lifting from the upper level shortwave and left entrance of the upper jet will hit early Saturday morning continuing into the early afternoon. Mountains snow will start to increase overnight Friday into Saturday, with the heaviest snow Saturday morning and early afternoon. There will be two potential big impacts to mountain travel on Saturday. The first potential impact is blowing snow. Wind gusts will be around 50 to 60mph at times, which when combined with fresh snow on the ground and snow falling around 0.5 to 1 inch an hour at times, could cause serious visibility issues. The second potential impact is snow squalls. Strong frontogenesis and some weak instability could be enough for snow squalls to develop in the mountains. Snow squalls cause rapid changes to visibilities and driving conditions, creating very hazardous travel. QPF amounts continue to trend higher for our higher elevations. This combined with the strong winds leading to blowing snow and the holiday weekend travel has led us to upgrade our Park Range zone to a Winter Storm Warning. As of right now, we've left our Front Range zones in a Winter Weather Advisory, due to the lower snow totals, but travel conditions could still be very hazardous if snow banding or snow squalls develop.

The timing of the cold front Saturday is still uncertain. A few of the high res models are trending faster, with the front entering our northern counties between 7 and 8am, reaching the metro around 9, and exiting our southern counties by 11am (which is before the GFS even brings it into our northern counties). If this happens, it would give the plains a much quicker transition from rain to snow and colder afternoon temperatures. We are leaning towards the quicker front solutions and have adjusted the forecast accordingly. A trace to a few tenths of snow still looks possible for the metro Saturday afternoon, but it will depend on that front timing. the south metro, Palmer, and southern foothills will be favored for better precip chances and snow totals given the north/northeast flow behind the front. We are also monitoring the potential for snow bands to develop due to the strong frontogenesis. Areas that see a heavier snow bands will be more likely for brief snow accumulations on roads and potential travel impacts.

Snow chances will decrease Saturday evening as the shortwave and jet move out of our area. Dry conditions will prevail Sunday through Tuesday for much of the area, with warmer temperature for the start of next week. We could see a weak upper level disturbance bring brief snow chances to the mountains on Monday, but little to no impacts are expected. Models are showing an upper level low developing off the southwest coast on Tuesday, moving east over the four corners and then near our area. The exact progression of the low is still uncertain in both timing and location, but this will be our next chance for both mountain and plains snowfall. Right now, the best chance for precip with this system will be late Wednesday into Thursday. Temperatures are forecast to drop back closer to normal behind the cold front associated with this system.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Sunday will start off chilly as skies clear overnight behind Saturday's system. Despite more sunshine, we will still have a cold airmass in place, which should keep highs down in the upper 30s to lower 40s.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Winds will increase through Friday night with gusts peaking to 65-70 mph at the wind-prone locations. Heavy mountain snow is expected Friday night into Saturday where gusty winds will persist.
- A strong cold front will sweep through the area Saturday morning, bringing colder temperatures and snow.
- Saturday's snowfall may be locally heavy, with reduced visibility in falling and blowing snow and minor accumulations impacting holiday travel.
- Another round of strong winds is possible (50% chance) in the wind prone areas Sunday through early Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: High winds continue across the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming early this morning. All four wind prone locations have verified, with 60 to 65 MPH gusts so far. High winds will continue through much of the day on Friday as a fast moving shortwave dips into Wyoming. This shortwave may turn winds northwest enough to drop winds below high wind criteria in Bordeaux. Northwest is not a favorable direction for high winds, thus the High Wind Warning for Bordeaux expires around 11 AM, roughly when the wind direction here shifts. This shortwave will, however, have the potential to bring high winds to the Laramie Valley and central Laramie County. 50 to 60 kt winds aloft with decent subsidence could bring these winds down to the surface. Cross-sections of omega and potential temperature also show a strong mountain wave signature which could cause high winds in these locations with any breaking waves. Even the NBM and GFS LAMP show fairly high gusts around Laramie and Cheyenne. However, in-house guidance does not show high probabilities for high winds in these location. Due to potential uncertainty in the magnitude of wind gusts, opted for a High Wind Watch for these zones in case a quick upgrade is needed if winds get close to criteria. High winds are expected to continue across Arlington and the South Laramie Range and foothills with steep CAG to CPR height gradients and strong subsidence facilitating gusts over 60 MPH. This fast moving shortwave will exit the CWA by the evening, weakening winds in the Laramie Valley and central Laramie County. As a result, High Wind Watches only go through 5 PM today for these areas.

At the heels of this shortwave, is another progressive, but moister shortwave. Ahead of this shortwave, winds aloft will increase over central and northern Carbon County Friday night. 55 kt winds aloft combined with decent subsidence could lead to high winds around Rawlins and Muddy Gap. Again, even the LAMP and NBM show favorable wind gusts, so went ahead and upgraded the High Wind Watches to Warnings for these locations. Strong winds will continue through Saturday morning, but will abruptly end by Saturday afternoon as a cold front quickly moves across the forecast area. The north winds behind the front are not favorable for high winds, but gusty conditions are still expected behind the front. Although High Wind Warnings for the wind prones continue through Saturday evening, it is likely that these could be cancelled early as models have sped up the timing of the cold front.

To go along with the wind on Saturday, this progressive shortwave will bring the chance for precipitation. Mountain snow is expected to start accumulating Friday night, with healthy snowfall rates leading to impressive accumulations within a short amount of time. The Sierra Madre Range is in a Winter Weather Advisory for about a foot of snowfall while the Snowy Range is in a Winter Storm Warning as it takes the brunt of the QPF. Accumulations between 8 and 16 inches are expected with locally higher amounts possible at higher elevations. These winter headlines will continue through Saturday evening. Accumulations for the lower elevations across the area will be hit or miss. Due to this being more of a clipper system, it is likely that accumulations for the lower elevations do not exceed more than a few inches. If precipitation starts as rain, it will likely transition quickly to snow as the front is quite strong. ECMWF and GFS ensembles are generally in good agreement with the GFS showing slightly higher snowfall totals. But anywhere from a trace to about 2 inches will be what most locations see. As winds turn more northerly, locations like Douglas, the Pine Ridge and Laramie could see more than 2 inches as upslope flow promotes good snowfall rates. Another area to watch for potential winter headlines will be the North Laramie Range has snowfall will be favorable with the north winds. Snow will taper off by Saturday evening, leading to a chilly overnight.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Sunday will start off chilly as skies clear overnight behind Saturday's system. Despite more sunshine, we will still have a cold airmass in place, which should keep highs down in the upper 30s to lower 40s. The flow aloft will start to turn more zonal Sunday onwards, which will increase the potential for strong winds in the wind prone areas once again. 700-mb height gradients are marginally supportive for high winds in the Arlington/Elk Mountain area during the day on Sunday, spreading eastward to the Laramie range wind prone areas Sunday night into Monday as surface pressure falls east of the range. Current probabilities are around 60 to 70% for the Arlington area, and 50% for the I-80 Summit and Bordeaux areas. Elsewhere, westerly flow will resume warm air advection as 700-mb temperatures climb back above 0C Monday and remain there through at least Wednesday. This should push highs back to around 5-10F above seasonal averages. Conditions look largely dry, though there may be another round of light mountain snow around Monday into Tuesday with a weak shortwave passing through.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Snow showers will taper off Sunday morning, with only a few orographically driven showers lingering along the Park Range under drying northwesterly flow. A transient ridge builds in Sunday into Monday, bringing quieter conditions seasonably mild temperatures.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow will begin along the northern Divide late Friday, lingering through Sunday morning. Snow totals of 10-14 inches are expected for the Park and Elkhead mountains, with 4-8 inches across the Flat Tops and Central Divide Mountains.
- Winds gusting up to 45 mph are expected with this evening, leading to blowing and drifting snow and difficult driving conditions over the mountain passes.
- An unsettled pattern looks to continue into next week with potential for more mountain snow, but details remain uncertain.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The ridge to our west is in the process of breaking down this evening, with increasing upper level moisture in the form of mid to high level clouds spilling in from the northwest. Aside from the clouds, seasonably mild temperatures and relatively quiet conditions will continue through the day Friday.

The first in a series of shortwaves in the northwesterly flow reaches eastern Utah and western Colorado Friday evening. Light snow showers are expected to begin along the Northern Divide and spread south through the night. The strongest in this series of waves arrives Saturday morning, with the highest snowfall rates expected between 5AM and 5PM Saturday. This will impact morning and evening commutes, as well as any post-Thanksgiving Holiday traffic over the mountain passes. A Winter Storm Warning has been issued for the Park and Elkhead mountains, and Winter Weather Advisories remain in effect for the Central Divide mountains and Flat Tops, all from 5PM Friday evening to 5AM Sunday morning. For the Park and Elkhead mountains, 10-14 inches of snow are expected, with locally higher amounts possible. For the Central Divide Mountains and the Flat Tops, snow totals of 4-8 inches are expected, with locally higher amounts possible. This system will also bring strong northwesterly winds capable of gusting to 45 mph. As a result, blowing and drifting snow will also be a concern. If planning on travelling at any point on Saturday, be prepared for difficult winter driving conditions, with blowing snow reducing visibility and slick, messy road conditions.

Snow showers will taper off Sunday morning, with only a few orographically driven showers lingering along the Park Range under drying northwesterly flow. A transient ridge builds in Sunday into Monday, bringing quieter conditions seasonably mild temperatures. This ridge flattens through the day Monday, with flow shifting from northwesterly to more zonal in response to a wave moving into the Pacific Northwest. Model confidence with the impact of this first wave remains low, however it is possible that increasing moisture and favorable orographics will result in some light snow showers along the Divide. Blended guidance has reasonably high probabilities (50-70%) of an inch or two of snow with this first wave. Looking towards the middle of the week, there is potential for a stronger, more southerly system to impact the Four Corners and southern mountains. Model guidance remains in relatively poor agreement, with significant spread. The southerly track does increase potential for atmospheric river moisture to accompany this system. However, the exact track of this system can make the difference between a solid mountain snowfall and seeing no snow at all. We shall have to wait and see how the forecast for this system develops over the coming days.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Wednesday into Friday...the next upper storm system is forecast to begin impacting the region Wednesday, with widespread precipitation possible Thursday into Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Warm today with 60s to near 70 degrees for highs, a few snow showers are forecast for the Central Mountains overnight.
- Snow increases across the Central Mountains where 3-7 inches are possible. A strong cold front is forecast for the Plains with winds 50 to 60 mph Saturday afternoon.
- First possible snow for the Plains mid to late next week???

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...satellite imagery early this morning shows mid and high cloud cover spreading south into Colorado due to embedded energy. This area of clouds will continue to spread south through sunrise. Temperatures have fallen into the 20s to lower 30s across the Plains, with a few areas along the Eastern Mountain lee slopes in the 40s. Temperatures will cool off a few more degrees through sunrise.

Today and tonight...northwest flow will shift more westerly by tonight, as an upper shortwave trough digs across Colorado. For today, strong mixing will allow for temperatures to warm nicely, with 60s to near 70 degrees across the Plains, and 50s for the San Luis Valley. Gusty winds will be possible in gap wind prone areas along the I-25 corridor, with gusts near 30 mph.

For tonight, energy begins to move into western Colorado, with a few light snow showers developing across the Central Mountains. Minor accumulations may be possible north of Cottonwood Pass by Saturday morning. Increased westerly flow will keep winds elevated for much of the region, helping to keep overnight lows mild in the 30s and 40s. Would not be surprised to see a few sites in the lee of the Eastern Mountains remaining near 50 degrees overnight.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Models in good agreement through the extended period, with a few differences for mid to late next week.
Saturday...a quick moving upper shortwave is forecast to track across Colorado on Saturday. This will bring a mix of weather to southern Colorado through Saturday night.

For the Continental Divide, snow showers are forecast Saturday and Saturday evening. A Winter Weather Advisory is in effect for the Central Mountains, where 3 to 7 inches of snow are possible, along with 55 mph wind gusts, with the highest accumulations north of Cottonwood Pass. This shower activity will peak Saturday afternoon, and dissipate through the overnight hours.

Conditions on the Palmer Divide could be briefly interesting. A very strong cold front is forecast to drop south by late morning. A warm start is expected, with temperatures falling quickly with the frontal passage, down into the lower to mid 30s. Very strong winds, 45 to 55 mph along with a band of rain changing to snow is expected with the frontal passage. There could be a period during the afternoon with brief heavy snow bursts and blowing snow conditions. Overall, snow amounts will be minor, less than an inch, but travel impacts due to poor visibility and slick road could cause problems. These conditions will need to be monitored for appropriate highlights, whether its short fused snow squall warnings or an advisory.

For the rest of the Plains, the cold front will rapidly drop south, clearing into New Mexico by early afternoon. This is significantly faster than previous model runs, which had it passing through by late afternoon. This may impact afternoon high temperatures, which may occur early, with highs along and south of Highway 50 in the lower 60s. Temperatures will rapidly fall behind the cold front, falling into the 40s by early evening. The main concern will be very strong winds. High Wind Watches are in place for portions of the Plains, where wind gusts could exceed 60 mph during the afternoon and early evening. Recent dry conditions could lead to areas of blowing dust, and strong cross winds on west-east highways will likely pose hazardous travel conditions. Model guidance continues to develop a narrow band of showers with the front as it pushes south. Given the earlier frontal passage, warmer temperatures will likely keep precip type as rain, with a few snow flakes possible near the Eastern Mountains and Raton Ridge. With the current model guidance, the main impacts will be from wind.

Sunday into Tuesday...flat upper ridging is forecast to move across Colorado for early next week. This will lead to daily breezy conditions in wind prone areas along the I-25 corridor. There could be a few snow showers along the Continental Divide with any weak embedded waves that move through the upper flow. Overall, temperatures will warm back into the 50s and 60s each afternoon.

Wednesday into Friday...the next upper storm system is forecast to begin impacting the region Wednesday, with widespread precipitation possible Thursday into Friday. All guidance has an upper system tracking across the region, with the main differences being storm track. The GFS is furthest north, while the ECMWF, Canadian and various ensemble and AI guidance are south. At this time, mountains look to see snowfall, with accumulations expected. On the Plains, the guidance with the southern tracks wrap a trowal south along the I-25 corridor with possibly our first snow of the winter season. Ensemble and deterministic guidance trends have shown some consistency over the past few model cycles.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Beyond this system, there is medium confidence that this wavetrain continues through the first to second week of December.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Temperatures will be increasingly mild for Friday, with maxes around 5-10F above seasonal normals.
- A weak storm system will move across northern Utah late Friday into Saturday, bringing generally light valley rain and mountain snow to northern Utah and southwest Wyoming.

- Dry conditions will return temporarily on Sunday, with a more active pattern resuming into the middle of the week. A potent area of low pressure looks to make impacts primarily across southern Utah, bringing high elevation snowfall and valley rain.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A weak area of high pressure remains steadfast over the region and will continue to do so through the next 24-hours. This area of high pressure will gradually weaken throughout the day on Friday, with weak shortwave impulses ushering in cooler air overhead. This decrease in temperatures overhead looks to aid in better mixing across the region, which will help to bring an increase in temperatures as valley inversions weaken. Increased moisture overhead from an active northern stream will also allow for increased cloud cover through the day on Friday.

This moisture, tied to an upstream atmospheric river, will continue to increase through Friday evening/ Saturday morning as the parent shortwave trough moves into the region. The existing inland-pentrating atmospheric river will weaken as the parent shortwave energy moves into northern Utah early Saturday morning. That said, the anomalous moisture will pair with the shortwave trough and interact with the high terrain in northern Utah to generate a period of high elevation snowfall and valley rain from roughly Salt Lake/ Tooele County northward. Depending on the overall depth of the trough, we could see precipitation extend as far south as the I-70 corridor (primarily in the high terrain), but the expected limited impacts will exist north of the I-80 corridor. Again, while impacts will be limited, a brief period of moderate high elevation snowfall and low elevation (<6,800ft) rain should be anticipated in the Bear River mountains and Ogden area mountains early Saturday morning. No headlines are expected to be issued at this time.

A brief period of ridging will round out the weekend, bringing stable conditions areawide on Sunday with mild temperatures expected throughout Utah and southwest Wyoming. Largely dry conditions will prevail through at least Tuesday morning across much of the area with the exception of the northern Bear Rivers. The aforementioned active northern stream looks to bring another round of light precipitation to this area from Monday afternoon through early Tuesday.

Focus of the forecast period will then shift to the Tuesday/Wednesday/Thursday timeframe as the persistent ridge we've been dealing with begins to break down, opening the door to much more potent areas of low pressure. Ensemble guidance is in fairly good agreement on a deep area of low pressure moving in from the eastern Pacific, tracking into the southwestern U.S. (textbook El Nino) from Tuesday through Thursday. While the ensemble means from the EPS and GEFS are in generally good agreement, there still exists a fairly high amount of spread when breaking down and clustering individual members. The biggest uncertainty at this time is figuring out how far south/north the low will pass... a farther northern track will allow for much more widespread valley rain and mountain snow (45% chance), whereas a more southern track (in line with ensemble means) would favor primary precipitation concerns across the southern half of Utah (55% chance). While odds are generally split, southern Utah still looks to fare better with precipitation totals from this system but the forecast spread remains high.

Beyond this system, there is medium confidence that this wavetrain continues through the first to second week of December. We'll need to see how things evolve throughout the week, but there looks to be a non-zero chance that we'll see our first decent chance at widespread lower elevation snowfall across Utah around December 6-8... something to keep and eye on!

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Near and above treeline, you can trigger an avalanche that is large enough to injure and bury you. Slopes that face the north half of the compass, and are steeper than about 30 degrees are the most suspect. Give slopes where recent storms drifted snow a wide berth; you might trigger them from above, next to, or below.
Seek out wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline for safer travel options.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: You can trigger a dangerous avalanche where you encounter older wind-drifted slabs below ridgelines, especially on northwest through north to east-facing slopes at upper elevations. You might trigger them from thin spots above, adjacent to, or below the drifted features. Choose wind-sheltered terrain to avoid the problem.
At this point, Saturday's storm does not look to raise the danger for this area. However, if the storm tracks further south it might. Check back Friday evening for a forecast update.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe from avalanches due to thin and discontinuous snow cover. You can trigger a small avalanche in wind-drifted snow above treeline. Look for these drifts below ridges and around rocky outcrops on slopes facing west through north to east.

2697.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe to travel on, as there is very little snow. In the alpine, steer around hard snow drifts on steep terrain below ridgetops.
A storm arrives on Friday night that will increase avalanche danger on Saturday.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

1736.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Elevations above 7,000 feet have 1-2 feet of snow on the ground. You may encounter pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north- and east-facing terrain. If the snow feels stiff or slabby underfoot, then find a different aspect away from wind-drifted snow. The biggest hazard remains thin snow cover and hitting rocks, logs, and stumps. Even a small slide through thin coverage could end a season before it even starts.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: Above 7,000 feet, a layered snowpack is beginning to build for the season. Good, albeit thin, skiing and riding conditions have been reported at upper elevations. Elevations below 7,000 feet remain thin and bony. Before November 13th, most slopes were bare. Winter trailhead access remains a challenge as there is not quite enough snow to launch sleds. Most forest roads become impassable by vehicle above 6,500 feet. As folks start poking around the mountains, remember that avalanches can occur with just a few feet of snow on the ground. There may be some lingering pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north and east-facing terrain features, particularly just below ridgelines.

Beginning Thanksgiving Day, a large storm system will impact the Pacific and Interior Northwest. Strong winds, mountain snow, and fluctuating rain/snow levels will be in the cards for several days. Pay attention to changing weather and snow conditions heading into the weekend. Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

Fresh wind slabs will come back onto the menu with more snow and wind later this week. Pay attention to gullies that can become crossloaded and may also act as a terrain trap. Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices. Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
Turn On Your Snow and Avalanche Brain

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).

• Help us paint a picture of what's going on in the mountains. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps forecasters and the public alike.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe to travel on, as there is very little snow. In the alpine, steer around hard snow drifts on steep terrain below ridgetops.
A storm arrives on Friday night that will increase avalanche danger on Saturday.
